The lower floor and roof are consistent with the reference style, so it passes.

answer.evidence: The main body is a two-storey half-timbered house. Its large hipped tile roof fills rows 6-45 and widens from 72 to 144 px as the roof slopes toward the viewer. The roof ends in a dark eave line at row 46 (L=22) with darker shadow rows 44-45 above it. Below it the south wall runs from row 47 to about row 111 (65 rows) with windows, a door and timber framing. The porch has its own sloped tile roof (rows ~82-97) over the entrance with its own front edge and shadow, and the front face continues below it down to the stem at rows 112-127. The hip-roof side slopes are part of the roof plane, not a receding side wall. The roof and porch both read clearly as top surfaces, so this matches the green references (a large top plane, a front-edge line and eave shadow, then the front face).

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate's tile roof has per-tile scallops with highlight, light, mid, dark and deep tones, about 5 steps, close to the references' 5-6. Half-timber beams are dark brown, and the plaster is speckled rather than flat. Outlines are dark red-brown beside the roof and dark brown beside the wood, with no uniform black line; only 7% of dark edge pixels are neutral, the same as h101. Measured facts: 16 visible tones per tile against 12 and 10 for the references, and 0% near-flat coverage, equal to the references. The windows have shutters, flower boxes and a lantern, and the porch roof repeats the tile texture. The only weakness is that the large two-storey wall is somewhat repetitive. It would sit next to the references without looking flatter or more sticker-like.
